15 In a large container in an oil refinery, three oils of different densities are mixed. No chemical
activity occurs.
The mixture consists of:
1200 kg of oil of density 1100 kg m–3
1500 kg of oil of density 860 kg m–3
4000 kg of oil of density 910 kg m–3.
What is the density of the mixture?
A
927 kg m–3
B
933 kg m–3
C
957 kg m–3
D
1045 kg m–3

hints: Notice you are given masses in $\text{kg}$ and densities in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$, so each oil occupies a different volume $V = m/\rho$.
Recall mixture density is total mass divided by total volume, not the average of the three density numbers.
Calculate the three separate volumes for the $1200 \text{ kg}$, $1500 \text{ kg}$ and $4000 \text{ kg}$ samples, add them, then divide $6700 \text{ kg}$ by that sum.
walkthrough: Total mass is the sum of the three masses: $m = 1200 + 1500 + 4000 = 6700 \text{ kg}$.
Use $\rho = m/V$ rearranged to $V = m/\rho$ for each oil with volumes in $\text{m}^3$.
Add volumes because there is no chemical activity or volume change: $V = 1.091 + 1.744 + 4.396 \approx 7.231 \text{ m}^3$.
Mixture density is $\rho = m/V = 6700/7.231 \approx 927 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$ with correct units. This is option A.

A.explanation: Total mass $6700 \text{ kg}$ divided by total volume about $7.23 \text{ m}^3$ gives about $927 \text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

B.explanation: This is close to the mass-weighted mean density, which is wrong because volumes add, not densities weighted by mass.

C.explanation: This is the simple mean of the three densities, which ignores the different masses and volumes of each oil.

D.explanation: This value is too high and above two of the components, suggesting total volume was underestimated or masses were added incorrectly.
